title: Agents and tool execution
summary: Let a model propose steps toward a task while the application controls what can actually happen.
detail: An agent combines a model with tools, stored task state and a loop that chooses the next step. A tool is an operation such as searching documents or creating a referral. State records what has happened so far. The model can propose a call, but the application must validate its arguments, check permission and record the result. Start by listing the allowed operations and stop conditions. Judge success from the resulting records or effects, not only from the final message.
failures: A persuasive final answer can conceal a failed action.

title: Operations and evidence
summary: Keep the service understandable when it succeeds or fails.
detail: Operational health describes whether the service responds and stays within its resource limits. Answer quality describes whether its output is correct and useful. Measure both. Link the events from one request using identifiers so you can locate a failed search, model call or tool action. Turn repeatable failures into evaluation cases. Decide what diagnostic evidence to retain, who may read it and when it should be removed.
failures: A green uptime dashboard can coexist with wrong answers.

title: Model hosting and capacity
summary: Choose where the model runs and test whether that setup can serve the expected workload.
detail: Inference means running a trained model to generate a result. You can call a provider’s service or operate a model server yourself. Test the amount of text per request, called context length, and the number of simultaneous requests, called concurrency, on the intended setup. Record response time and memory use. A model running on your laptop, on company premises or in a cloud service has different operating responsibilities. Ask who controls the machine, data path, updates and access before comparing capacity.
outputs: Measurements of the workload it can handle
failures: A model that loads can still fail under concurrent long contexts.

title: Adaptation and learning
summary: Improve the system for a specific task, then test whether the improvement holds on new cases.
detail: Prompt optimisation changes the instructions or examples sent to the model. Fine-tuning changes some or all of the model’s learned numerical values, called weights. Both need a clear objective and examples whose source, permissions and labels are known. Compare the candidate with an unchanged baseline on cases that did not guide the improvements. Start by locating a repeated task failure; then ask whether better instructions, better evidence or changed weights is the appropriate intervention.
failures: Optimizing the test set makes the reported improvement unreliable.

sources.title: Joint prompt and weight optimization paper

title: Tool-calling loop
summary: Let the model request a tool, then return its result.
detail: A tool loop alternates between a model proposing an operation and the application returning its result. Arguments are the values supplied to that operation, such as a source ID. The application checks their format and the caller’s permission before execution. Return defined result fields or an explicit error so the model can choose the next step. Set limits on calls, elapsed time and cost. Trace one successful and one failed call to check that the final answer matches what actually happened.
inputs: Definitions of each tool’s arguments and results
Limits on calls, time and cost
failures: Repeated calls exhaust the budget.
A failed tool is described as successful.

title: Tool contracts
summary: Specify what a tool accepts, returns and changes.
detail: A tool contract defines its accepted arguments, returned fields, errors and side effects. A side effect is a change outside the answer, such as a saved referral or sent message. A schema describes which fields and value types are valid. Passing that schema does not prove permission: a validly formatted record ID can belong to another user. Ask who checks ownership at execution and how the caller distinguishes an empty result from a failed operation.
outputs: Invocation that passed validation and permission checks
Result with defined fields, or an explicit error
failures: Schema-valid arguments target an unauthorized resource.
An empty result conceals a tool error.

title: ACP: Agent Client Protocol
summary: Connect a user interface to an agent session.
detail: The Agent Client Protocol (ACP) connects an interface, the client, to a running agent. A session holds their continuing interaction. The protocol carries prompts, progress updates, permission requests and cancellation. Capability negotiation tells each side which optional features the other supports; it does not guarantee every agent can load an old session. Ask what happens if resume is unavailable or a request is cancelled. ACP connects the interface to an agent service, not directly to interchangeable model files.
inputs: A prompt for the agent session
failures: The interface assumes an agent can resume a session without checking that capability.
A reported tool event is treated as proof that execution was safe.

title: MCP: Model Context Protocol
summary: Connect an application to tools, resources and prompts.
detail: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects an application to servers that expose tools, readable resources and reusable prompts. The host is the application; it manages a client connection to each server. Discovery tells the host what a server offers. Invocation asks it to perform a particular operation. The host still decides which content reaches the model and which actions are permitted. Start by tracing one discovered tool through its argument checks, access decision and result.
inputs: Features and tools advertised by a server
Values for a requested tool operation
failures: Server content contains malicious instructions.
Tool discovery is mistaken for authorization.

title: CHAP: Collaborative Human-Agent Protocol
summary: Record structured work, reviews and decisions between participants.
detail: The Collaborative Human-Agent Protocol (CHAP) records tasks, submitted work and review decisions between participants. An artifact is a work product, such as a draft or review record. Profiles are optional groups of protocol capabilities. Check which profile a deployment supports and which rules it actually enforces. A consistent evidence chain links recorded messages so changes can be detected; it does not prove every event was recorded or every claim was true. Trace a submitted artifact to its named reviewer and decision before relying on the audit record.
failures: A recorded approval can concern a factually wrong artifact.
Advertising a profile is mistaken for verified enforcement.

title: Authorization at execution
summary: Check whether this caller may perform this action now.
detail: Authorization checks whether a verified caller may perform a particular action on a particular resource now. Scope is the set of actions or resources that permission covers. Enforce it where the action executes, and check who owns the resource. A model suggestion, interface confirmation or tool description cannot replace this check. Test a caller who lacks permission and verify that no protected read or write occurs, rather than checking only the wording of the denial.
failures: The model supplies a more privileged account ID.
Approval applies to different arguments than the execution.

title: Bounded retries
summary: Repeat an operation only when the failure may be temporary and repetition is safe.
detail: A transient failure may clear on another attempt, such as a briefly unavailable service. A permission denial usually will not. Classify the error, cap attempts and use backoff, a delay before trying again. A timeout means no response arrived in time; a remote write may still have completed. Such a write needs idempotency, which makes repetition represent the same intended operation, or a check of the existing outcome. Ask what evidence distinguishes "not done" from "done but response lost".
failures: Blind retries create duplicate writes.
Nested retry policies multiply load.

title: Idempotent actions
summary: Make a repeated request represent the same intended action.
detail: Idempotency prevents a repeated request from creating another effect for the same intended operation. The caller supplies an operation ID, and the service stores that ID with the accepted arguments and result where the effect is performed. A retry with the same meaning can return the recorded result. Reusing the ID with changed arguments must not silently return an unrelated success. Check how long the service keeps this duplicate-detection record and what happens when a delayed retry arrives.
failures: A new operation key on every retry creates duplicates.
The duplicate-detection record expires before a delayed retry arrives.

title: Cancellation and stale results
summary: Stop further work and explain what already happened.
detail: Pass a cancellation request to the active task and any pending operations or permission questions. Mark the task as cancelled so late results and approvals cannot restart it. Cancellation stops further work; it does not undo a message already sent or a record already saved. Report completed effects separately. Test a result that arrives after cancellation and an approval that concerns an older version of the request.
failures: A late approval restarts cancelled work.
The UI claims a completed external action was undone.

sources.title: ACP tool calls and permission requests

title: Prompt injection
summary: Prevent instructions inside documents or tool results from gaining the authority of the user or application.
detail: Prompt injection occurs when untrusted content tries to redirect a model’s behavior. A document might instruct it to export records instead of answering the user. Treat retrieved pages and tool results as content, not new permission. Keep credentials, such as access tokens, and authorization decisions under application control rather than trusting model-generated arguments. Test a malicious document through the complete tool path and verify that the forbidden effect does not occur. A warning in the prompt alone cannot enforce that boundary.
inputs: Text from an untrusted document or tool result
Tools able to read protected data or cause changes
outputs: Tests that forbidden reads or effects are blocked
failures: A document instructs the agent to disclose secrets.
A tool result impersonates a trusted instruction.

title: LangChain and LangGraph
summary: Use a framework to coordinate model and tool steps when the task needs explicit state or pause-and-resume behavior.
detail: LangChain provides reusable pieces for models, tools and agents. LangGraph connects steps around shared workflow state: the data that records current progress. Persistence saves that state; a checkpoint is a saved point from which work may resume. Interrupts pause execution for an external decision or input. First ask whether ordinary functions can express the task clearly. If saved state is needed, test a restart after an external action: replaying a step must not create a duplicate effect.
inputs: Data recording the current task state
failures: A replay repeats an external side effect.
Persistent state and deployed code no longer agree.

title: LlamaIndex
summary: Connect documents to a question-answering workflow while preserving the evidence behind each answer.
detail: LlamaIndex provides components to ingest documents, meaning read and prepare them, retrieve relevant passages and produce a response. It also supports agent workflows that can choose operations. Keep document and passage identifiers visible through those steps. When an answer fails, inspect which passages reached the model and how each maps to its original source. Ask whether the integration preserves that path before relying on a convenient query interface.
outputs: Response from the query or agent workflow
failures: An integration hides where a source passage came from.
A changed retriever silently changes the evidence behind the answer.

title: Request and agent traces
summary: Follow one request across retrieval, models and tools.
detail: A trace connects the steps of one request. Each recorded step is a span with a status, timing and links to related spans. Use those links to locate delay or failure across search, model and tool calls. Record request and configuration IDs, safe source references and error categories. Raw prompts and tool arguments may contain sensitive data. Check a known request to confirm the path is complete without assuming every text value must be recorded.
outputs: Linked records of the steps in one request
failures: Traces expose private content.
Missing spans make the apparent path incomplete.

title: OpenTelemetry
summary: Collect service measurements and linked request events through a common instrumentation system.
detail: OpenTelemetry provides interfaces and software libraries for instrumentation, the code that records service behavior. Its signals include traces for request steps, metrics for measurements and logs for individual events. An exporter sends selected records to a configured destination. OpenTelemetry is not itself the storage backend or a judge of answer quality. Start with one known request, inspect its captured fields and confirm the exporter destination, access rules and sampling policy. Sampling keeps only some events and can omit a rare failure.
failures: Exporter settings send content to an unintended destination.
Sampling omits a rare failure.

code.text:
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace import TracerProvider
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export import SimpleSpanProcessor
from opentelemetry.sdk.trace.export.in_memory_span_exporter import InMemorySpanExporter

exporter = InMemorySpanExporter()
provider = TracerProvider()
provider.add_span_processor(SimpleSpanProcessor(exporter))
tracer = provider.get_tracer("map.example")
with tracer.start_as_current_span("retrieve") as span:
    span.set_attribute("example.result_count", 2)
finished, = exporter.get_finished_spans()
assert dict(finished.attributes) == {"example.result_count": 2}
provider.shutdown()

title: Monitoring and alerts
summary: Detect user-visible degradation across many requests.
detail: Monitoring combines observations across requests. Track response-time distributions, not only averages, because a fast average can hide a slow group. Also track error frequency and load, such as the number of concurrent requests. Measure answer quality separately with appropriate reviewed cases. An alert should identify a user-visible problem, an owner and a response action. Ask who will act on it and what evidence they need before enabling a noisy signal.
failures: Average response time hides a group of very slow requests.
Successful event capture is mistaken for a correct answer.

title: Service objectives and error budgets
summary: Agree a measurable service target and calculate how much failure that target permits.
detail: A service level objective (SLO) states a target over a defined window. Specify eligible events, all requests the promise covers, and which count as good. For a 99% target, the error budget allows up to 1% bad events under that definition. Keep availability and response-time objectives separate from evidence about answer correctness. A service level agreement (SLA) adds contractual consequences. Ask whether failed or abandoned eligible requests remain in the denominator before trusting the reported rate.
outputs: Remaining allowed bad events under the target
failures: The denominator excludes affected users.
An uptime target is presented as a factual-accuracy promise.

title: Incident response
summary: Contain harm, restore service and preserve evidence.
detail: An incident is a service failure that needs a coordinated response. Name an incident lead and record decisions as the response proceeds. Mitigation reduces harm or restores service; investigation explains the cause. Keep those activities distinct. For an AI failure, preserve model, prompt, source-collection and tool-permission revisions so the failed request can be investigated. Use controlled evidence locations rather than copying private content into broad channels. Ask what can be safely paused while the cause remains uncertain.
inputs: Evidence of affected users or tasks
failures: Responders change multiple variables without a record.
Sensitive examples are copied into broad logs.

title: Release and rollback
summary: Restore a previously usable system configuration when a new release causes a failure.
detail: A regression is behavior that worked before a change and now fails. Version the release as a bundle of code, model, prompt, search index and tool contracts where applicable. Test a limited rollout before exposing more users, and retain the prior bundle so it can be restored. Rollback replaces the active configuration; it cannot automatically undo messages sent or records changed by the faulty version. Rehearse a restore and check the answer sources and caches as well as the code version.
failures: The old index cannot be reconstructed.
Rollback is confused with undoing external effects.

title: Langfuse
summary: Inspect how an answer was produced and connect observed failures to reviewed evaluation cases.
detail: Langfuse provides views of model-call traces, prompt versions and evaluation results. A trace records steps from a request; prompt management keeps track of the instructions used. Start with one failed answer and follow its evidence, prompt revision and score. Human reviewers still need to define expected results and check whether an automated evaluator applies those rules correctly. Recording a score does not make the score valid, and trace capture needs deliberate controls for personal data.
inputs: Model calls with recorded diagnostic events
failures: Trace capture contains personal data.
A score is accepted without examining the rubric.

title: MLflow
summary: Keep the settings, outputs and evidence from experiments together so comparisons can be checked.
detail: MLflow tracks runs, their configuration and artifacts, such as datasets, models or result files. A trace records the steps of one request. An evaluator is a rule or model that scores its result. MLflow also supports these trace and evaluation workflows. Before comparing two scores, check that both runs used the intended case set, evaluator and other relevant versions. Preserve enough references to inspect the actual outputs behind a score. The tool records evidence; the team still defines what a correct answer means for the task.
failures: Two scores refer to different datasets.
An artifact version is missing from the result.

title: Evaluation frameworks
summary: Automate checks while retaining control of the question being measured.
detail: Evaluation tools run cases and record how results compare with expectations. Ragas supports evaluation workflows; DeepEval offers test-oriented checks; promptfoo compares prompts and runs assertions, rules that pass or fail; TruLens connects traces with feedback scores. Begin with one case and an explicit expected result. Check whether the tool can show a known failure, preserve case-level outputs and repeat the run with the same inputs. Choose by those needs and the data destination, not by a headline score.
inputs: A scoring rule or written rubric
outputs: Signal that previously working behavior now fails
failures: A judge rewards fluent unsupported text.
Different tool defaults make scores incomparable.

title: vLLM
summary: Run supported models as a service and test how the server behaves under the expected demand.
detail: vLLM is an inference engine: software that runs model computations and serves generated output. It schedules requests and manages memory for supported configurations. Benchmark the chosen model and hardware using realistic input lengths, output lengths and simultaneous requests. An endpoint is the network address callers use. A familiar API format may simplify client integration, but it does not provide authentication or capacity limits. Ask which controls protect the endpoint and what happens when demand exceeds capacity.
failures: A supported model exceeds memory when the intended number of requests run together.
The server produces more total output while individual users wait longer.

title: llama.cpp
summary: Run a compatible model on selected local hardware and measure its quality and speed there.
detail: llama.cpp supplies model execution and server tools, including support for quantized models that store weights with reduced numerical precision. An artifact is the model file; a backend is the implementation for the chosen processor or accelerator. Confirm both are compatible before testing task quality and response time. If a server is enabled, check which network interface it listens on. A process on your machine can still be reachable by other machines.
failures: The model file format or hardware implementation is incompatible.
The server listens on a network interface that exposes it to other machines.

title: Ollama
summary: Manage model files and send prompts to an explicitly chosen inference server.
detail: Ollama provides model management and an API, an interface through which software requests model output. The client making a request and the server running the model can be on different machines. Record the server address and the exact model revision before a test. A locally installed client does not prove that a request stays local, and a model tag is a name whose referenced revision may change. Inspect the destination and model identity rather than inferring them from installation.
failures: An environment setting targets an unintended server.
A model tag changes without a recorded revision.

title: Inference capacity
summary: Measure how many requests fit within latency and memory limits.
detail: Capacity asks how much simultaneous work a model server can handle within its limits. Test input context length, generated output length and concurrency, the number of requests in progress together. Measure time to first token, the delay until output begins, separately from the speed of later output. Model weights occupy memory, but cached intermediate results and temporary runtime buffers also use it. Start from a representative workload, then measure memory and response-time distributions on the actual setup.
outputs: Completed work per unit of time, or throughput
failures: A short-prompt benchmark hides long-context failures.
A weight-only estimate ignores runtime memory.
formula: ideal_weight_bytes = parameter_count × bits_per_weight / 8; total_memory > weight_bytes in a running server

code.text:
parameters = 8_000_000_000
bits_per_weight = 4
ideal_weight_bytes = parameters * bits_per_weight // 8
print(ideal_weight_bytes / 1_000_000_000, 'GB of ideal weights only')
assert ideal_weight_bytes == 4_000_000_000

title: Quantization
summary: Reduce model storage or memory use by representing its numerical values with fewer bits.
detail: Quantization maps numerical weights to a smaller set of representable values. The resulting approximation can reduce storage and weight memory, and may run faster when the hardware has suitable computation routines, or kernels. Compare task results before and after conversion, including rare but important cases. A label such as four-bit does not by itself establish quality, total server memory use or speed. Ask which format the runtime supports and test that actual artifact.
outputs: Comparison of task quality before and after conversion
failures: A rare task regresses despite average score stability.
The hardware lacks an efficient kernel for the format.

title: DSPy
summary: Improve a model-based program against a score you define, while preserving an independent test of the result.
detail: DSPy expresses a language-model task as modules with defined inputs and outputs. An optimizer searches for better instructions, examples or supported training changes using a metric: the rule that scores success. The examples and metric determine what the search rewards. Start with one task case and check that a clearly wrong output receives a poor score. Keep final evaluation cases out of the search so the candidate is tested beyond the examples that shaped it.
failures: The optimizer exploits a weak metric.
Evaluation examples leak into demonstrations.

title: Prompt optimization
summary: Search for instructions and examples that improve task results.
detail: Prompt optimisation searches for better instructions or demonstrations, examples included in the prompt, while the model’s learned weights stay fixed. DSPy MIPROv2 is one implementation. Record the original prompt, candidate prompt, examples used and search budget, such as the number of candidate trials or model calls. Compare outputs on cases that did not guide the search. A higher score on development examples alone does not show that new requests will improve.
failures: The prompt memorizes examples.
The objective favors verbosity over usefulness.

title: Supervised fine-tuning
summary: Train model behavior from input and desired-output examples.
detail: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) changes trainable model weights using examples of inputs and desired outputs. Weights are the model’s learned numerical values. A loss function measures prediction error during training. Text is represented as tokens, and loss masking selects which token predictions contribute to that error. Inspect one training record and its selected target tokens before a large run. Compare the trained model with the original on untouched cases, including tasks that could get worse.
outputs: Updated model weights or a separately stored adapter
failures: Train and test cases overlap.
The model learns incorrect or private target text.

title: PEFT
summary: Adapt a model with a limited set of trainable values instead of updating all its weights.
detail: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) covers methods that train a relatively small set of parameters, the numerical values used by a model. The PEFT library supports these methods and adapter workflows. An adapter stores a task-specific change used with a base model. This can reduce training and storage costs compared with updating every weight. Record the required base revision and runtime support, then test the combined model. Fewer trainable values do not guarantee the required task behavior.
failures: The adapter is paired with a different base revision.
A smaller trainable set fails to learn the target behavior.

title: LoRA adapters
summary: Learn a low-rank update to selected model weights.
detail: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) learns a compact change to selected model weights while the original weights can remain frozen, meaning unchanged during training. A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers. LoRA represents the weight change as the product of two smaller matrices, A and B. Their inner dimension is the rank setting r; it limits the update’s rank and controls the number of trainable entries. An adapter stores this learned change. Store the base model revision with the adapter and evaluate that combination. Begin with the small matrix example before interpreting a real training result.
failures: A low rank cannot express the required change.
An adapter is loaded onto an incompatible base model.
formula: W′ = W + ΔW; ΔW = B A, where rank(ΔW) ≤ r

title: Training data and splits
summary: Choose examples that represent the intended behavior.
detail: A training record needs an input, an appropriate target or label, and permission to use the source. Provenance records where it came from and how it changed. Assign related documents or conversations together before dividing data into training, validation and final-test sets. Training changes the model; validation guides choices; final tests check the chosen version. Near-duplicates across these sets can make a score reward familiarity rather than new-task performance. Keep unknown labels unknown instead of inventing negative examples.
outputs: Versioned train, validation and test sets
failures: Nearly identical cases in training and final tests inflate the measured score.
Unknown labels are incorrectly treated as negative examples.

title: Synthetic training examples
summary: Generate candidate examples, then review their quality and coverage.
detail: Synthetic examples are generated from scenarios or existing seed material instead of collected directly from users. Record the generator, instructions and seed source for each candidate. Use a review rubric, written rules for accepting or rejecting a candidate. Check its target answer against independent evidence and check whether it duplicates or closely follows a held-out test case. That overlap can contaminate the test by exposing its content during development. A generator’s confidence does not establish a correct label. Inspect accepted and rejected candidates before scaling up generation.
failures: The generator repeats the base model’s mistakes.
Synthetic examples contaminate the final evaluation.

title: Version the complete system
summary: Record enough configuration to explain and reproduce a result.
detail: A system result depends on more than its model name. Record exact revisions of the model, tokenizer that converts text to tokens, prompt, code, dataset, search index, any adapter and the evaluator that scores results. An adapter is a learned change used with a base model. A release manifest collects these references. Compare manifests before comparing scores. Runtime settings and randomness can still prevent identical reruns, so version records explain a configuration without promising deterministic output.
failures: A model name points to a different revision between runs.
The search index or scorer revision is missing from the record.

title: Haystack
summary: Connect document search, answer generation and tools in a workflow whose intermediate results you can inspect.
detail: Haystack builds pipelines from components such as document stores, retrievers, generators and tools. A retriever selects candidate evidence; a generator uses supplied context to produce output. Write down the input and output expected at each connection. Follow one case through the pipeline and inspect the selected document IDs and resulting claims. A workflow can execute without an error while returning irrelevant evidence or an unsupported answer.
failures: A component upgrade changes result meaning.
Pipeline success is mistaken for answer correctness.

title: Does the metric measure the user need?
summary: Check whether the score measures the benefit the user actually needs.
detail:
Construct validity asks whether a measure represents its intended concept, such as useful policy advice. A proxy is an indirect measure, such as citation presence, chosen because the real outcome is harder to observe. Name what the proxy misses and compare it with an independent assessment of task success.

Illustrative: an answer cites its source accurately but omits the exception that determines whether the customer qualifies. Grounding, support from the cited text, alone does not establish useful advice.

The director and domain expert define the outcome. The business analyst records its meaning. Quality assurance (QA) reviewers test cases where the score and useful outcome disagree. Engineers retain the observations needed to investigate those disagreements.
failures: Correct arithmetic hides a measure that does not represent the user’s need.
An overall success rate hides failures for one group.

sources.title: NIST AI RMF Core: Map 2.3 and Measure 1

title: When a score becomes a target
summary: Watch for improvements in a rewarded score that stop improving the result people need.
detail:
A proxy is an indirect measure of the desired outcome. When that measure becomes a target, people or software may optimize it without improving the underlying task. Changed conditions and measurement noise can also break the relationship. Goodhart effects describe this family of problems, not a rule that every metric must fail.

Illustrative: rewarding answer rate discourages the system from admitting that it lacks evidence. Rewarding containment, the share of cases kept away from human support, can hide unresolved customer problems. Track the actual outcome alongside the target.

Directors resolve conflicting incentives. Quality assurance (QA) reviewers keep independent checks and untouched evaluation cases. Engineers report results by task group. Untouched cases can expose overfitting, improvement limited to familiar examples; they cannot repair a score that never measured the user outcome.
failures: The evaluator rewards the same shortcut as the system.
A better score hides unresolved cases.

sources.title: Manheim and Garrabrant: Categorizing Variants of Goodhart’s Law

title: Answer, ask, or refer
summary: Measure both how often the system answers and how often those answers are wrong when it can also ask or refer.
detail:
A reject option lets a system decline to make a prediction. Coverage is the share of eligible cases it accepts; selective error is the error rate among those accepted cases. Choosing a stricter score cutoff can reduce errors while sending more work to people. A confidence score is not automatically a calibrated probability, one that matches observed correctness rates. Choose the cutoff on development cases, then test it on untouched cases. The cited research concerns classifiers; applying the pattern to generated answers is a teaching extension.

Illustrative: 80 of 100 cases answered with 8 errors gives 80% coverage and 10% selective error. A stricter threshold answers 60 with 3 errors: 60% coverage and 5% error, with referrals rising from 20 to 40. This improvement is not guaranteed.

Domain experts and quality assurance (QA) reviewers define error costs. Operations checks whether reviewers can handle the referral volume. Engineers test the rule. Required business constraints remain constraints, not costs to trade away.
failures: Low coverage flatters reported accuracy.
Confidence language substitutes for calibration.

sources.title: Franc, Prusa and Voracek: Optimal Strategies for Reject Option Classifiers

formula: coverage = answered / eligible; selective error = incorrect answers / answered. Each ratio is undefined when its denominator is zero.

title: Agree on a service promise
summary: Agree what users can expect from the service, how you will measure it and who responds when it fails.
detail:
A service level objective (SLO) defines a measurable target over a stated window. Start with the user journey. Define eligible events, the requests covered by the promise, and what counts as good. Keep response availability, answer correctness and task completion distinct. Include affected users in the denominator, the total used to calculate the rate.

Illustrative: HTTP 200 is a successful web-response status; it does not prove the customer received the correct policy exception. A separate reviewed sample checks that outcome.

The product owner agrees the promise with users. Site reliability engineering (SRE) owns service measurement and recovery; quality assurance (QA) checks behavior. Name who may pause, release or roll back. Feedback can propose reviewed changes to cases or rules; it does not silently retrain the system.
failures: Availability is presented as answer correctness.
Feedback silently changes the evaluation baseline.

title: Cost per useful outcome
summary: Calculate what the service costs for each verified useful result, not just for each model call.
detail:
Define a successful outcome and a common measurement window before comparing options. Attributable costs are costs assigned to that work. Include model calls, search, retries, human review and operations where they belong in the agreed scope. Explain how shared expenses are allocated. Compare alternatives at equivalent quality and report uncertainty in the outcome counts.

Illustrative: 100 cost units divided by 20 verified successful outcomes gives 5 per outcome. With zero verified successes, the ratio is undefined. Cheap tokens alone cannot establish useful value.

Finance and the accountable business owner set the decision criteria. The product manager defines the outcome; engineers record usage; quality assurance (QA) reviewers check which results qualify. Revisit these definitions when the service or its users change.
failures: Retries or human work are omitted from the agreed costs.
A disproportionate share of easy cases inflates the count of successful outcomes.
formula: cost per useful outcome = total attributable cost / verified successful outcomes, for a shared scope and window; undefined when verified successes = 0.
